Main.sentence: The Congressional Black Caucus ( CBC ) is made up of Black members of the ___E:United States Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ .

Representative ___E:Yvette Clarke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvette_Clarke)___ from ___E:New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state))___ , the current chairperson, succeeded ___E:Steven Horsford U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Horsford)___ from ___E:Nevada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada)___ in 2025. Although most members belong to the ___E:Democratic Party U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ , the CBC founders envisioned it as a non-partisan organization, and there have been several instances of bipartisan collaboration with ___E:Republicans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ .

The predecessor to the ___E:caucus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucus)___ was founded in January 1969 as the Democratic Select Committee by a group of black members of the ___E:House of Representatives U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ , including ___E:Charles Diggs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Diggs)___ of Michigan, ___E:Shirley Chisholm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Chisholm)___ of New York, ___E:Louis Stokes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Stokes)___ of ___E:Ohio U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio)___ , and ___E:Bill Clay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clay)___ of ___E:Missouri U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri)___ .

As a result of Congressional redistricting and the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s, more black representatives were elected to the House (increasing from nine to thirteen), encouraging them to establish a formal organization.
Diggs, who is acknowledged that to have proposed the Democratic Select Committee,  would serve as its chairman from 1969 to 1971.
During a meeting between committee members on February 2, 1971, a motion put forward by Clay to transform the Democratic Select Committee into a formal, non-partisan caucus for African American U.S.
Congress members was accepted.

During the same meeting, the organization, on the motion of ___E:Charles Rangel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Rangel)___ of New York,  then changed its name to the Congressional Black Caucus.

The thirteen founding members of the caucus were ___E:Shirley Chisholm U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Chisholm)___ , ___E:Bill Clay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clay)___ , ___E:George W. Collins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Collins)___ , ___E:John Conyers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Conyers)___ , ___E:Ron Dellums U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Dellums)___ , ___E:Charles Diggs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Diggs)___ , ___E:Augustus Hawkins U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_Hawkins)___ , ___E:Ralph Metcalfe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Metcalfe)___ , ___E:Parren Mitchell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parren_Mitchell)___ , ___E:Robert N. C. Nix Sr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_N._C._Nix_Sr.)___ , ___E:Charles Rangel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Rangel)___ , ___E:Louis Stokes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Stokes)___ , and Washington, D.C., delegate ___E:Walter Fauntroy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Fauntroy)___ .
Diggs served as its first chairman from 1971 to 1972.  Chisholm referred to the group as "unbought and unbossed".

Five founding members of the CBC were also members of ___E:Prince Hall Freemasonry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Hall_Freemasonry)___ , an African-American branch of ___E:Freemasonry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freemasonry)___ that became involved in civil rights: Stokes, Conyers, Rangel, Hawkins and Metcalfe.

President ___E:Richard Nixon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon)___ refused to meet with the newly formed group, leading the CBC to boycott the 1971 ___E:State of the Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_Union)___ address.

After their first joint press conference, Nixon finally met with the CBC on March 25, 1971. The Caucus presented the President with a 32-page document including "recommendations to eradicate racism, provide quality housing for black families, and promote the full engagement of blacks in government".
All the members of the caucus were included on the ___E:master list of Nixon political opponents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_list_of_Nixon_political_opponents)___ . [citation needed]

On June 5, 1972, shortly before the ___E:1972 Democratic National Convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Democratic_National_Convention)___ nominated ___E:George McGovern U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_McGovern)___ for president, the CBC released two documents: the ___E:Black Declaration of Independence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Black_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&redlink=1)___ and the ___E:Black Bill of Rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Black_Bill_of_Rights&action=edit&redlink=1)___ .  ___E:Louis Stokes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Stokes)___ read a preamble and both documents into the record of the House of Representatives.

The Black Bill of Rights includes sections on jobs and the economy, foreign policy, education, housing, public health, minority enterprise, drugs, prison reform, black representation in government, civil rights, voting rights in the District of Columbia, and the military.

These documents were inspired by the ___E:National Black Political Convention U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Black_Political_Convention)___ and its own manifesto, The Gary Declaration: Black Politics at the Crossroads  (also called the Black Agenda).

In 1977, the organization was involved in the founding of ___E:TransAfrica U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TransAfrica)___ , an education and advocacy affiliate that was formed to act as a resource on information on the African continent and its Diaspora.

They worked closely with this organization to start the national anti- ___E:apartheid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid)___ movement in the US, ___E:Free South Africa Movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_South_Africa_Movement)___ (characterized by sit-ins, student protests, it became the longest-lasting civil disobedience movement in U.S. history) and to devise the legislative strategy for the ___E:Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensive_Anti-Apartheid_Act)___ of 1986 that was subsequently passed over ___E:Ronald Reagan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan)___ 's veto.

In late 1994, after ___E:Republicans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ ___E:attained a majority in the House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Revolution)___ , the House passed House Resolution 6 on January 4, 1995, which prohibited “the establishment or continuation of any legislative service organization..."  This decision was aimed at 28 organizations, which received taxpayer funding and occupied offices at the Capitol, including the CBC. Then-chairman ___E:Kweisi Mfume U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kweisi_Mfume)___ protested the decision.
The CBC reconstituted as a Congressional Member Organization.
The caucus is sometimes invited to the ___E:White House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House)___ to meet with the president.
It requests such a meeting at the beginning of each Congress.

During the ___E:2020 George Floyd protests U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Floyd_protests)___ , the CBC provided ___E:House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives)___ members with ___E:stoles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stole_(vestment))___ made from ___E:kente U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kente)___ to be worn for an ___E:8:46 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight_minutes_46_seconds)___ -long ___E:moment of silence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_of_silence)___ before introducing the ___E:Justice in Policing Act of 2020 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_in_Policing_Act_of_2020)___ .

The ___E:caucus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_caucus)___ describes its goals as "positively influencing the course of events pertinent to African Americans and others of similar experience and situation", and "achieving greater equity for persons of African descent in the design and content of domestic and international programs and services."

The CBC encapsulates these goals in the following priorities: closing the achievement and opportunity gaps in education, assuring quality health care for every American, focusing on employment and economic security, ensuring justice for all, retirement security for all Americans, increasing welfare funds, and increasing equity in foreign policy.
Representative ___E:Eddie Bernice Johnson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Bernice_Johnson)___ (D–TX), has said:
The Congressional Black Caucus is one of the world's most esteemed bodies, with a history of positive activism unparalleled in our nation's history.
Whether the issue is popular or unpopular, simple or complex, the CBC has fought for thirty years to protect the fundamentals of democracy.
Its impact is recognized throughout the world.
The Congressional Black Caucus is probably the closest group of legislators on the Hill. We work together almost incessantly, we are friends and, more importantly, a family of freedom fighters.
Our diversity makes us stronger, and the expertise of all of our members has helped us be effective beyond our numbers.

___E:Mark Anthony Neal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Anthony_Neal)___ , a professor of ___E:African-American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American)___ studies and popular culture at ___E:Duke University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University)___ , wrote a column in late 2008 that the Congressional Black Caucus and other African-American-centered organizations are still needed, and should take advantage of "the political will that ___E:Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obama)___ 's campaign has generated."

The Congressional Black Caucus PAC is a ___E:political action committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee)___ founded as a political arm of the caucus, aiming "to increase the number of Black Members of the US Congress...support Non-Black Candidates who will champion the needs and interests of the Black Community" and increase the "participation of Black Americans in the political process".  ___E:Gregory Meeks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregory_Meeks)___ (D- ___E:NY-5 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York%27s_5th_congressional_district)___ ) chairs the PAC. The CBCPAC is known for its ___E:moderate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moderate_politics)___ -lean.  The PAC caused controversy when it backed incumbent ___E:Michael Capuano U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Capuano)___ , a white man, over challenger ___E:Ayanna Pressley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayanna_Pressley)___ , a black woman who ultimately defeated him.  Two years later, it backed ___E:Eliot Engel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Engel)___ , a white incumbent, over ___E:Jamaal Bowman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaal_Bowman)___ , a black challenger who went on to defeat him.

___E:HuffPost U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost)___ reporters questioned how endorsements were made, noting that the executive board included corporate ___E:lobbyists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbyists)___ over CBC members.

Representative ___E:Brenda Lawrence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brenda_Lawrence)___ (D- ___E:MI-14 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan%27s_14th_congressional_district)___ ) criticized the PAC's endorsement policies in 2020 and called for it to be reevaluated.  ___E:Color of Change U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_of_Change)___ , a ___E:civil rights U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_and_political_rights)___ advocacy ___E:nonprofit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit)___ group, released a letter in 2016 calling on the CBCPAC to cut ties with lobbyists from industries that are "notorious for the mistreatment and exploitation of Black people" including ___E:private prisons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_prisons)___ , ___E:pharmaceutical companies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical_companies)___ , ___E:student loan creditors U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_loans_in_the_United_States)___ , and ___E:big tobacco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_tobacco)___ .
The caucus has grown steadily as more black members have been elected.
At its formal founding in 1971, the caucus had thirteen members.

As of 2023, it had 55 members, including two who are non-voting members of the House, representing the ___E:District of Columbia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia)___ and the ___E:U.S. Virgin Islands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Virgin_Islands)___ .
As of 2025, there have been twelve black senators since the caucus's founding.

The ten black U.S. senators, all Democrats, who are or have been members of the Congressional Black Caucus are Senator Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, elected in 2024 (currently serving), Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware, elected in 2024 (currently serving), Senator ___E:Cory Booker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cory_Booker)___ of New Jersey, elected in 2013 (currently serving), Senator ___E:Raphael Warnock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphael_Warnock)___ of Georgia, elected in 2021 (currently serving), and Senator ___E:Kamala Harris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris)___ of California, elected in 2016, who resigned in 2021 to take on the vice presidency; former senators ___E:Carol Moseley Braun U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Moseley_Braun)___ (1993–1999), ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ (2005–2008), and ___E:Roland Burris U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roland_Burris)___ (2008–2010), all of Illinois; former senator ___E:Laphonza Butler U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laphonza_Butler)___ (2023–2024) of California, and former senator ___E:Mo Cowan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Cowan)___ (2013) of Massachusetts.

Burris was appointed by ___E:Illinois governor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Illinois)___ ___E:Rod Blagojevich U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Blagojevich)___ in December 2008 to fill Obama's seat for the remaining two years of his Senate term after Obama was elected ___E:president of the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States)___ .
Cowan was appointed to temporarily serve until a special election after ___E:John Kerry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry)___ vacated his Senate seat to become U.S. secretary of state.

Senator ___E:Edward Brooke U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Brooke)___ , a Republican who represented Massachusetts in the 1960s and 1970s, was not a member of the CBC. In 2013, Senator ___E:Tim Scott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Scott)___ , Republican of South Carolina, also chose not to join the CBC after being appointed to fill ___E:Jim DeMint U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_DeMint)___ 's Senate seat.

The caucus is officially non-partisan; but, in practice, the vast majority of Black politicians elected to Congress since the CBC's founding have been ___E:Democrats U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Democratic_Party)___ .

Twelve Black ___E:Republicans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Republican_Party)___ have been elected to Congress since the caucus was founded in 1971. Of those, only ___E:Delegate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delegate_(United_States_Congress))___ ___E:Melvin H. Evans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_H._Evans)___ of the Virgin Islands (1979–1981), Representative ___E:Gary Franks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Franks)___ of Connecticut (1991–1997), Representative ___E:Allen West U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_West_(politician))___ of Florida (2011–2013), and Representative ___E:Mia Love U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mia_Love)___ of Utah (2015–2019) joined the CBC.
Edward Brooke was the only serving Black U.S. senator when the CBC was founded in 1971, but he never joined the group and sometimes clashed with its leaders.

In 1979 ___E:Melvin H. Evans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_H._Evans)___ , a non-voting delegate from the Virgin Islands, became the first Republican member in the group's history. ___E:Gary Franks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Franks)___ was the first Republican voting congressman to join in 1991, though he was at times excluded from CBC strategy sessions, skipped meetings, and threatened to quit the caucus.

___E:J. C. Watts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._C._Watts)___ did not join the CBC when he entered Congress in 1995, and after Franks left Congress in 1997, no Republicans joined the CBC for fourteen years until ___E:Allen West U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_West_(politician))___ joined the caucus in 2011, though fellow freshman congressman ___E:Tim Scott U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Scott)___ declined to join.  After West was defeated for re-election, the CBC became a Democrat-only caucus once again in 2013.
In ___E:2014 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections)___ , two black Republicans were elected to the House.

Upon taking office, ___E:Will Hurd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Hurd)___ from Texas declined to join the caucus, while ___E:Mia Love U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mia_Love)___ from Utah, the first black Republican congresswoman, joined.
In 2021, newly elected black Republican ___E:Byron Donalds U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byron_Donalds)___ was blocked from joining the CBC.

All past and present members of the caucus have been Black. [citation needed] In 2006, while running for Congress in a ___E:Tennessee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee)___ district which is 60% black, ___E:Steve Cohen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Cohen_(politician))___ , who is white, pledged to apply for membership in order to represent his constituents.
However, after his election, his application was refused.
Although the bylaws of the caucus do not make race a prerequisite for membership, former and current members of the caucus agreed that the group should remain "exclusively black".

In response to the decision, Cohen referred to his campaign promise as "a social ___E:faux pas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faux_pas)___ " because "It's their caucus and they do things their way. You don't force your way in. You need to be invited."

Representative ___E:Lacy Clay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacy_Clay)___ , a Democrat from Missouri and the son of Representative ___E:Bill Clay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clay)___ , a co-founder of the caucus, said: "Mr. Cohen asked for admission, and he got his answer.
He is white and the caucus is black.
It is time to move on. We have racial policies to pursue and we are pursuing them, as Mr. Cohen has learned.
It is an unwritten rule. It is understood." Clay also issued the following statement:

Quite simply, Representative Cohen will have to accept what the rest of the country will have to accept—there has been an unofficial Congressional White Caucus for over 200 years, and now it is our turn to say who can join 'the club.' He does not, and cannot, meet the membership criteria unless he can change his skin color.
Primarily, we are concerned with the needs and concerns of the black population, and we will not allow white America to infringe on those objectives.

Later the same week, Representative ___E:Tom Tancredo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Tancredo)___ , a Republican from Colorado, objected to the continued existence of the CBC as well as the ___E:Democratic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States))___ ___E:Congressional Hispanic Caucus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Hispanic_Caucus)___ and the ___E:Republican U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States))___ ___E:Congressional Hispanic Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Hispanic_Conference)___ arguing that "It is utterly hypocritical for Congress to extol the virtues of a color-blind society while officially sanctioning caucuses that are based solely on race. If we are serious about achieving the goal of a colorblind society, Congress should lead by example and end these divisive, race-based caucuses."
Prior to 2017, no one had attempted to be in both the CBC and the ___E:Congressional Hispanic Caucus U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Hispanic_Caucus)___ (CHC).

In the ___E:2016 House elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_New_York#District_13)___ , Afro-Dominican State Senator ___E:Adriano Espaillat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Espaillat)___ was elected to an open seat after twice trying to unseat CBC founder ___E:Charlie Rangel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Rangel)___ (who also has Puerto Rican ancestry) in the Democratic primary.

Espaillat signaled that he wanted to join the CBC as well as the CHC, but it was reported that he was rebuffed, and it was insinuated that the cause was bad blood over the attempted primary challenges of Rangel.

In the ___E:2018 elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_New_York#District_19)___ , Afro-Latino Democrat ___E:Antonio Delgado U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Delgado_(politician))___ was elected and joined the CBC, making no public effort to join the CHC as well. In the ___E:2020 elections U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_New_York#District_15)___ , Afro-Puerto Rican Democratic candidate ___E:Ritchie Torres U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritchie_Torres)___ published an ___E:op-ed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Op-ed)___ claiming that he was prevented from joining both the CBC and CHC as he wished to do,  a claim which was denied by then-CBC chair ___E:Karen Bass U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Bass)___ .
After being elected to Congress, Torres successfully joined both the CBC and CHC.

The Congressional Caucus on Black Women and Girls is a separate caucus of the United States Congress founded in 2016 to advance issues and legislation important to the welfare of women and girls of African descent.
